title: Raymond James Raised Its NVIDIA Target to $352
summary: Raymond James lifted NVIDIA to a $352 target on August 25, and the reason is not the GPU: it is CPUs, a line the firm expects to grow from roughly 3% of sales to 5% by 2028. Four Wall Street targets now sit between $325 and $352. On our own Form 4 record this month, no NVIDIA insider has bought a single share on the open market.
body:
Key points

  • Raymond James raised its NVIDIA price target from $330 to $352 on August 25, keeping a Strong Buy rating. The stock was trading near $213 at the time — the target implies roughly 65% upside.
  • The call is not about GPUs. Raymond James expects CPU revenue to grow from about 3% of NVIDIA's sales today to 5% by calendar 2028, calling CPUs the fastest-growing element in its model and arguing NVIDIA could become the world's largest CPU revenue leader within several years.
  • Wall Street is crowded on the same side: Cantor Fitzgerald $350, KeyBanc $330, Rosenblatt $325. On our Form 4 record, the only NVIDIA insider activity this month has been equity awards and a 500,000-share gift — and not one open-market purchase.

Price targets tell you what analysts think a stock is worth. Form 4 filings tell you what the people running the company are doing with their own money. On NVIDIA right now, those two records are not saying the same thing — and the gap is worth understanding before you read the target as a signal.

The call: a CPU story hiding inside a GPU company

Raymond James lifted its NVIDIA target to $352 from $330 on August 25 and kept its Strong Buy rating. What makes the note unusual is the driver. Almost every bull case written on NVIDIA in the last three years has been a data-centre GPU case. This one leans on the processor line most investors have stopped thinking about.

The firm's own framing was blunt: "CPUs are not a new part of Nvidia's business" — but the company has, in Raymond James' words, "increased its visibility in the segment, particularly with agentic use cases." The model has CPU revenue moving from roughly 3% of total sales today to about 5% by calendar 2028, and the analyst describes that line as the fastest-growing element in the model. Extend the trajectory and Raymond James believes NVIDIA could end up the global leader in CPU revenue within several years.

That matters more than the percentage suggests. Five percent of NVIDIA's sales is not a rounding error at a company carrying a $5.1 trillion market capitalisation — it is a business the size of a large-cap semiconductor company appearing inside an existing one, in a segment where the incumbents have spent two decades assuming the competitive map was settled.

The valuation argument

The $352 target is built on 22 times calendar 2028 earnings. The more striking number in the note is where the stock trades today: under 15 times calendar 2027 GAAP earnings, against 18.6 times for the S&P 500 as a whole. On that basis the most-discussed stock of the decade is priced at a discount to the index.

It is also a stock that has stopped outrunning the market. NVIDIA is up roughly 12% year to date — in line with the S&P 500, not ahead of it. Against a five-year median forward multiple of about 35 times, the compression is the whole argument: the earnings kept climbing and the multiple did not.

Where the rest of the street sits

Raymond James is not an outlier. The recent target cluster reads:

  • Raymond James — $352, Strong Buy
  • Cantor Fitzgerald — $350, Overweight
  • KeyBanc — $330, Overweight
  • Rosenblatt Securities — $325, Buy

Four firms, one direction, a $27 spread between the highest and lowest target. That is consensus, not conviction. When the entire published street sits inside a narrow band above the current price, the marginal information in any one upgrade is small — which is exactly when it pays to check a second, independent record.

What NVIDIA's own insiders have actually filed

Here is the part the price targets will not tell you. Across the NVIDIA Form 4 filings on our record this month, there has not been a single open-market purchase by an officer or director. What there has been:

  • August 10 — director Suzanne Nora Johnson received two equity awards totalling 2,410 shares. Awards are compensation. Nobody wrote a cheque.
  • August 5 — director Tench Coxe filed a gift of 500,000 shares, worth roughly $106 million at the current price. A gift is not a sale — no proceeds change hands, and transfers of this kind are routinely made to family trusts or charitable vehicles. But it is also not a purchase.

This is why NVIDIA carries no Insider Score on our platform. The score exists only where there are qualifying open-market buys to measure, and NVIDIA has not produced one. That is not a bearish reading — it is an absence of the specific signal we track, and the two should never be confused.

How to read the gap

None of this contradicts Raymond James. A CPU line compounding toward 5% of revenue is a genuine, checkable thesis, and sub-15x forward earnings on a business of this quality is a real argument. Analysts are paid to model the future of the business. Insiders file when they act on the present.

The honest reading is narrower than either a bull or bear case: the analyst record and the insider record are answering different questions. At a $5.1 trillion market capitalisation, executives already hold enormous equity through awards — the incentive to buy more in the open market is structurally weak in a way it simply is not at a $500 million company, where a CEO writing a seven-figure personal cheque is a decision rather than a formality.

So take the target for what it is: four firms, aligned, on a thesis about processors. And note what has not happened alongside it. When insider conviction does show up at a company this size, it is unmistakable — and it has not shown up here.

You can audit all of it yourself: NVIDIA's full filing history, today's actual open-market buying on Top Insider Scores, the IQS Screener for companies where insiders are buying with real conviction, and the analyst ratings tracker.

Not investment advice. Insider transactions are summarized from public SEC Form 4 filings on our own record; price targets, ratings, valuation multiples and analyst quotes are attributed to the public reporting cited above.
